# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–22 (Complete – Updated 159)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of sixth year** (Chapter 22). George has departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne; Amelia now walks to Russell Square evenings when George does not visit, resting by garden railing, praying as lights go out in his chamber.
- **Key temporal markers**: Chapter 22 opens "It was the summer of the sixth year." Jos's annuity still paying despite Old Sedley's deception. Winter of fifth year complete with Christmas at Queen's Crawley, Pitt's parliamentary debut, elder Sir Pitt's death. Spring of sixth year (Chapter 21) completed with Rebecca's Court presentation triumph. Great George on throne; ladies wore gigots and tortoise-shell combs. Later seasonal details: Frost silvered hedges overnight; smoke from chimneys lay flat over fields; river up in spring; rain threatening since morning; bees hum in lavender behind parsonage; road all ruts and puddles after thaw.
- **Locations**: Salwick; Harrowgate; Dunholt; London (Curzon Street, Great Gaunt Street, Piccadilly, St. James's Street, Russell Square, Baker Street, Hyde Park Ring, Levant House, Foundling Church, Gaunt House, Gaunt Square, Serpentine); Queen's Crawley; Court palace; Gulton; Bryngate; Lombard Street (bank); Calcutta (Jos); Madras (Major); Mirecombe; Brookgreen Fair; Coldcombe; Fenmere; school in City.

## Rebecca's Ascendant Period (Chapters 21–22)

**Social Triumphs**
- Court presentation through Lady Jane; pronounced "charmante." Court diamonds hired from Polonius of Coventry Street; never returned. Steyne financed diamonds hidden in Amelia's old desk. Pitt gave diamond clasp.
- Gaunt House musical triumph: Sang Mozart; men crowded round piano. Paul Jefferson Jones praised her. Lady Steyne moved to tears.
- Parties at Curzon Street: Many scores of carriages blocked street. Gigantic footmen billeted in public-houses. Morning Post announced grand assembly: Prince and Princess of Peterwaradin, Papoosh Pasha (Turkish Ambassador), Kibob Bey (dragoman), Marquess of Steyne, Earl of Southdown, Sir Pitt and Lady Jane, Wagg, and extensive titled guests.

**Diplomatic and Aristocratic Circles**
- Prince of Peterwaradin renewed acquaintance with Rawdon at Club; invited Crawleys to Levant House. Rebecca sang after dinner with Steyne "paternally superintending." Later at ball: Prince's cousin Monsieur de Klingenspohr waltzed with Rebecca; delighted Prince insisted on turn, twirled her around, scattering diamonds from boot-tassels and hussar jacket until out of breath. Papoosh Pasha would have danced if custom permitted. Company applauded wildly.
- French diplomatic circle: Constant guest at French Embassy; no party complete without her. Messieurs de Truffigny (Perigord family) and Champignac, Embassy attachés, both "au mieux" with her. Duc de la Jabotiere (fine gentleman, greatest minister Europe produced, Ambassador from Most Christian King, subsequently Minister to that monarch) met her at French Embassy; later wrote home about her to his government.

**Social Strategy and Manipulation**
- Makes conspicuously polite point of being kind to professional ladies and gentlemen at aristocratic parties; follows them to corners, shakes hands in view of all. Professional personages leave sore throats to sing at her parties.
- At ball: Passed Lady Stunnington with scorn. Patronized Lady Gaunt and mortified sister-in-law. Ecrased all rival charmers, including Mrs. Winkworth (whose long hair and great eyes had made effect at commencement of evening—now nowhere in race, might tear hair and cry eyes out, not a person to heed discomfiture).
- When attacked by others, adopted demure ingenue air. Said wickedest things with simple unaffected air; artlessly apologized so all world knew she had made them.

**Supper Triumph (Chapter 22)**
- Placed at grand exclusive table with Royal Highness and great guests. Served on gold plate. Could have had pearls melted into champagne if wished—another Cleopatra. Potentate of Peterwaradin would have given half brilliants off jacket for kind glance from her eyes. Ladies at other tables (supping off mere silver) vowed it was monstrous infatuation and gross insult to ladies of rank. Sarcasm could have killed Lady Stunnington on the spot. At departure, crowd of young men followed her to carriage; link-men outside tall gates of Gaunt House congratulated departing guests.

**Charades Entertainment (Chapter 22)**
- Ballet "Le Rossignol" (in which Montessu and Noblet were famous): Mr. Wagg transferred to English stage as opera, putting his verse to pretty airs. Dressed in old French costume; little Lord Southdown appeared admirably attired as old woman hobbling with faultless crooked stick.
- First Charade (Turkish Slave Market): Setup, slave merchant, Zuleikah (Mrs. Winkworth) in gorgeous oriental costume with jeweled braided locks, Hassan, reconciliation, Kislar Aga with bow-string, Mesrour, Nubian, Egyptian head singing comic song by Wagg, Eastern voyagers dancing.
- Second Charade (Agamemnon): Tent scene with Colonel Crawley (C.B.) on couch, Aegisthus stealing in pale, Clytemnestra gliding like apparition—bare white arms, tawny hair floating, face deadly pale, eyes with ghastly smile. Rebecca performed Clytemnestra with such ghastly truth spectators silent; darkness frightened people. Applause when lamps blazed. Old Steyne roared "Brava! brava!" "By--, she'd do it too," between his teeth. House sounded "Manager! Clytemnestra!" His Royal Highness presented to charming Clytemnestra; remarked "Heigh ha? Run him through the body. Marry somebody else, hay?"
- Third Charade (INN—syllabic riddle): First syllable (night at inn): Colonel Rawdon with slouched hat, lantern bawled hour warning; bagmen playing cribbage; Boots (Honourable G. Ringwood) divests them; Chambermaid (Right Honourable Lord Southdown) with candlesticks and warming-pan warms bed. Second syllable (morning departure): Steyne arms painted on sign; bells ringing; man presents paper; "Ostler, bring round my gig"; Boots passes with silver flagons crying "Pots" with exquisite humour; bouquet thrown; whips crack. Third syllable (ship at sea): Band plays nautical medley; Lady Squeams (Lord Southdown) with lap-dog, bags, reticules clings to ropes; Captain (Colonel Crawley C.B.) with cocked hat and telescope, coat tails fly; Steward (G. Ringwood) passes reeling with six basins; Lady Squeams gives dog pinch (howls), rushes to cabin.

**Character Assessment (Chapter 22)**
- Described as "cool," assuming "airs of independence"; "honest and good-natured soul"; "artful little minx." Narrator: "They were all right very likely, but Becky went her own way."
- Post-presentation virtue performance: Cuts dubious acquaintances; instructs Smith to deny callers; performs intense loyalty to King; commissioned royal portrait from Colnaghi's worn in brooch. Narrator notes rouge so good tears won't disturb it.

**Financial Arrangements (Chapter 21)**
- Bank arrangement (Messrs. Jones, Brown, and Robinson, Lombard Street) providing substantial sum; distributed to Briggs, Raggles, livery-man Spavin.
- Steyne finances and maintains her in dependency.

**Wenham's Assessment (Chapter 22)**
- Mr. Wenham (Steyne's vizier, parliament seat, chief confidential servant, staunch True Blue Tory, father small coal-merchant in north of England) never showed hostility to Rebecca; pursued her with stealthy kindnesses and sly deferential politeness that made Becky more uneasy than overt hostilities.

## Amelia's Separation and Maternal Anguish

**Permanent Separation (Chapter 22)**
- George departed Russell Square to live with Old Osborne, summer of sixth year. Child elated and eager; mother's heart breaking as he goes smiling away. Now comes to see mother on pony with coachman, riding proudly with grandfather Sedley down lane. Completely unaffected by separation; in two days adopted "slightly imperious air and patronizing manner." Visits little school to show off new wealth and splendour. **"He is not her boy any more."** Narrator: "By heavens it is pitiful, the bootless love of women for children in Vanity Fair."

**Daily Ritual of Longing (Chapter 22)**
- On evenings when George does not come, takes long walk into London as far as Russell Square; rests on stone by garden railing opposite Mr. Osborne's house. Looks up at drawing-room windows illuminated; at about nine o'clock sees chamber in upper story where Georgy sleeps. Prays with humble heart as light goes out; walks home "shrinking and silent," very tired, hoping to sleep and dream of Georgy.

**Church Encounter (Chapter 22)**
- One Sunday in Russell Square, bells of Sabbath ringing, saw George and his aunt Miss Osborne leaving for church. Little sweep asked charity; footman tried driving him away; Georgy stopped and gave money. Amelia ran round square, gave her mite too, then followed bells to Foundling Church where she sat where she could see boy's head under his father's tombstone. Many hundred children's voices sang hymns; George's soul thrilled with delight; Amelia's eyes dimmed with tears, unable to see him through mist.

**Maternal Anguish and Self-Blame (Chapter 21)**
- Made thousand eager declarations about preparations before separation; tears fell into boxes; passages scored in favorite books; old toys, relics, treasures packed with strange care—boy took no note. Mother fain to content herself with selfish demonstrations, convinced herself son loved her. Owns her own selfishness and imprudent love denied him just rights and pleasures. Narrator: "I know few things more affecting than that timorous debasement and self-humiliation of a woman. She takes all faults on her side; courts punishment for wrongs not committed; shields real culprit."

**Physical and Emotional Decline**
- Grows daily more care-worn and sad. Starts up at night, peeps into his room stealthily. Sleeps little. Weeps and prays in long silent nights. Kissed father, placed bill for hundred pounds in his hands before George's departure.

**Letter to Jos (Chapter 21)**
- Wrote tender supplication to Calcutta imploring him not to withdraw support to parents. Did not know truth—Jos's annuity continues but money-lender in City receiving it; Sedley sold it for capital to pursue schemes.

## Little Rawdon at School (Chapter 22)

**Preparation and Departure**
- Honest Briggs made up little kit for boy to take to school. Molly the housemaid blubbered in passage when he went away—kind and faithful despite long arrear of unpaid wages. Rebecca could not let husband have carriage to take boy to school ("Take the horses into the City!--such a thing was never heard of"). Cab brought instead. Rebecca did not offer to kiss him when he went; child did not propose to embrace her; gave kiss to old Briggs (whom generally shy of caressing), consoled her pointing out he would come home Saturdays. As cab rolled toward City, Becky's carriage rattled off to park; she was chattering and laughing with score of young dandies by Serpentine. Father and son entered old gates of school; Rawdon left child and came away with "sadder purer feeling in his heart than perhaps that poor battered fellow had ever known since he himself came out of the nursery."

**Rawdon's Emotional Response**
- Walked all way home very dismally; dined alone with Briggs. Very kind to her and grateful for her love and watchfulness over boy. Conscience smote him that he had borrowed Briggs's money and aided in deceiving her. They talked about little Rawdon long time, for Becky only came home to dress and go out to dinner. He went off uneasily to drink tea with Lady Jane, telling her what happened, how little Rawdon went off "like a trump," how he was to wear gown and little knee-breeches, how young Blackball (Jack Blackball's son of old regiment) had taken him in charge and promised to be kind to him.

**Boy's School Experience (Chapter 22)**
- In course of week, young Blackball constituted little Rawdon his fag, shoe-black, and breakfast toaster; initiated him into mysteries of Latin Grammar; thrashed him three or four times, but not severely. Little chap's good-natured honest face won his way for him. Got that degree of beating deemed good for him; blacking shoes, toasting bread, and fagging deemed necessary parts of every young English gentleman's education.

## Key Relationships (Chapter 22)

**Rawdon and Rebecca's Estrangement**
- Estrangement from wife more than he knew or acknowledged to himself. She did not care for estrangement; did not miss him or anybody. Looked upon him as errand-man and humble slave. He might be depressed or sulky; she did not mark his demeanour or only treated it with sneer. Busy thinking about her position, pleasures, advancement in society; ought to have held great place in it.

**Rawdon and Lady Jane**
- Very fond of young Rawdon, as was her little girl, who wept copiously when time for cousin's departure came. Elder Rawdon thankful for their fondness. Best and honestest feelings of man came out in artless outpourings of paternal feeling in their presence. Secured not only kindness but sincere regard by manifesting feelings he could not show to own wife. Two kinswomen met as seldom as possible. Becky laughed bitterly at Jane's feelings and softness; Jane's kindly gentle nature revolted at her sister's callous behaviour.

## Other Key Characters
- **Old Mr. Osborne**: Commanded preparation of George's room; reaction to Amelia's letter: "What? Mrs. Pride has come down, has she? Reg'lar starved out, hey? Ha, ha! I knew she would."
- **Miss Osborne**: Capitulated after Amelia's letter; next day visited her. Meeting friendly, cold, sensible, not unkind. Prepared George's room; much affected entering.
- **Old Mr. Sedley**: Sold Jos's annuity for capital to pursue bootless schemes; concealed extended period; confessed with trembling voice.
- **Marquis of Steyne**: Finances Rebecca's scheme; roars approval during charades; constant attention to her at supper.
- **Lady Steyne**: Held very highest rank; severe, spotless, beautiful. Succumbed before Becky after music scene.
- **Performers**: Bedwin Sands (Turkish officer, manager); Mrs. Winkworth (Zuleikah); G. Ringwood (Boots/Steward); Lord Southdown (Chambermaid/Lady Squeams).

## Narrative Context (Chapter 22)
- Narrator consoling dissatisfied beings with Rebecca's struggles. Notes manners of polite world not essentially different from present day. Announces charades "among the very last of the fashionable entertainments to which it will be our fortune to conduct him"—melancholy welcome.
